messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark is a 56-year-old professional dancer who has performed with a regional company for over three decades. He lives with his wife in a quiet suburb, and until six months ago, he considered himself lucky—a man who had built a career doing what he loved. Then, one evening on the way to a rehearsal, a familiar song came on the radio, and he glanced down to adjust the volume. In that split second, his car drifted across the lane and struck a cyclist at the edge of the road. The man was airlifted to the hospital with a traumatic brain injury and multiple fractures. Mark was not charged, but he has not been the same since.

Certain songs now stop him cold. When that same melody drifts from a passing car or a coffee shop speaker, his chest tightens and he is immediately back in the moment—the jolt, the thud, the silence afterward. He has come to believe that he will never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. He should have been paying attention; he should have swerved differently, hit the brakes sooner. The guilt is so sharp that it reshapes everything: he sees the accident as proof that he failed to protect someone who needed protecting, and that he has failed in his most important role in life—the role of a person who causes no harm. Those appraisals amplify the triggers. Now he is hyperaware of any sound that could be a crash, any sudden movement near the road, and he interprets these as fresh reminders that he is a person who hurt another.

To manage the unbearable feelings, Mark tries not to think about the trauma. He changes the station when certain songs play, and he refuses to drive past the intersection where it happened. He also dwells on how he used to be before the event—the dancer who moved with confidence, who could relax after a show, who trusted his own reactions. This dwelling creates a hollow ache, and the effort of suppression keeps his nervous system on edge. He has difficulty falling asleep because he needs to stay alert, listening for sounds he might have caused, even at home where he knows he is safe. His wife has noticed he cannot relax, and his focus in rehearsals has all but vanished; he misses counts, loses his balance, and the director has started giving him simpler roles.

The constant threat monitoring feeds back into the triggers. Because Mark is always scanning for danger, he is more likely to notice crowded spaces and interpret them as suffocating, more likely to flinch at a car braking too hard, more likely to be flooded by guilt when that song inevitably comes on. The cycle tightens: a trigger sparks the appraisal that he failed; the appraisal drives him to avoid and suppress; avoidance maintains his hypervigilance; hypervigilance makes him more sensitive to triggers. He feels trapped.

Last month, after he left a dress rehearsal early because a dancer backstage played a playlist that included the song, his wife insisted he see someone. Mark is afraid that if he stops suppressing, he will fall apart. But he is also terrified of losing his career—dancing is all he has known—and of the widening distance between him and the man he used to be. He wants to feel safe in his own body again, and to believe he deserves to move forward.
